week.t: NASA and Nature: Webb data clinch a first-of-its-kind stellar merger in Andromeda, caught as it happened
NASA and SpaceX stand down from the Dragon undocking over bad weather off California; new target Friday 12:05 pm US Eastern
NIST shows quantum physics and the speed of light can verify where a person is, with stations 195 m apart
Science News Explores: a Delft drone perches like a bird using touch, not cameras, in 26 out of 26 tests
NOAA Fisheries: 49 sightings of killer whale groups in the deep Gulf since 1978; one male seen across 26 years
Meteorological Service Singapore: Northeast Monsoon to set in during the second half of November; 94.2 mm in a day at Rivervale Drive on 6 Nov

tiles.cap: Two stars in Andromeda merged, and telescopes watched the whole seven-year plunge
tiles.nums: the Sun’s radius: the size of Big Bao, the giant star that swallowed its small companion
tiles.p1: A giant star in the Andromeda galaxy brightened for about seven years and swelled to more than twice its size while its surface temperature barely changed. Then, on 17 October 2025, it erupted. NASA says the data from Webb and six other telescopes clinch what happened: a small star of about 0.7 solar masses spiralled into its giant companion of about 7 solar masses, 350 times the Sun’s radius and 18,000 times as bright, and the two merged.
tiles.p2: Why now: the result was published in Nature on 18 November. Webb took its infrared look on 24 December 2025, 47 days after the peak.
deep: Seven orbits, seven years

The two stars had orbited each other for millennia. NASA says the final plunge took about seven orbits, roughly seven years. NEOWISE first flagged the star as variable in February 2023, and the Zwicky Transient Facility caught the eruption on 17 October 2025. Science News reports that when astronomers went back through nearly 30 years of data, the brightening had begun in 2018.
Why it counts as a merger

Only about a tenth of the giant’s outer gas is estimated to have escaped, and the energy of the fast-moving ejected gas suggests Little Bao reached Big Bao’s core. Karel Temmink of Radboud University called the giant “an absolute beast of a star, completely outshining its companion in the data.” Kishalay De of Columbia said it was “almost like a bomb exploding inside a living star.”
Hard to catch

Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University, who led the Nature paper: “Stellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict.” Dust now hides the system, so the final outcome may not be settled for years or decades. His next step: “Now we can go and try to look for similar systems.”
The name and the picture

The event’s designation is AT 2025abao, so the team nicknamed the pair Big Bao and Little Bao. The seven telescopes were NEOWISE, WINTER, SPHEREx, ZTF, Swift, Gemini North and Webb. The image is from the NASA Webb release, credit NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Viraj Karambelkar and Kishalay De (Columbia); processing Alyssa Pagan (STScI).
tiles.src: NASA Webb, NASA Data Clinches First-of-Its-Kind Stellar Merger, 18 Nov 2026 · Science News, Two stars in the Andromeda galaxy merged before astronomers’ eyes, 18 Nov 2026 (Meghan Bartels)
tiles.credit: Photo: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI / V. Karambelkar, K. De; processing A. Pagan

tiles.cap: Bad weather off California kept the Dragon on the station. Next try: 1:05 am Saturday here
tiles.nums: US Eastern on Friday 20 November, 1:05 am Saturday in Singapore: the earliest new undocking time, weather permitting
tiles.p1: NASA and SpaceX stood down from Wednesday’s undocking “due to unfavorable weather conditions at the splashdown sites off the coast of California,” NASA’s station blog said. The updated advisory now gives no earlier than 12:05 pm US Eastern on Friday 20 November for the cargo Dragon to leave Harmony’s space-facing port, which is 1:05 am on Saturday in Singapore, with live coverage from 11:45 am Eastern. Splashdown off California is set for no earlier than 5:04 pm Eastern on Saturday 21 November, 6:04 am on Sunday here, and NASA will not stream it.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: this Dragon arrived on 15 October with more than 6,300 pounds of supplies and goes home with frozen science and a broken robot part, so the packing in orbit went on while the weather decided.
deep: What is in the freezers

NASA lists a 3D-bioprinted blood-vessel construct, built to probe how blood vessels age; frozen tumour organoids that were treated aboard the station, for research into improving cancer treatments; frozen microbe samples from research into how antibiotic-resistant bacteria survive, adapt and evolve in space; and a lighting system coming home after more than three years, tested for its effect on astronauts’ sleep.
A robot wrist comes home

NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins packed the failed Canadarm2 wrist joint, replaced during the 30 June spacewalk, in protective covers for analysis on Earth. A spacesuit is also coming down for refurbishment. Watkins and Luke Delaney collected crew blood samples and loaded research samples into freezers; Anil Menon moved cargo from the Kibo module into Dragon; Canada’s Joshua Kutryk prepared protein crystal samples for a JAXA pharmaceutical experiment.
Why the ground does it

Dragon is a cargo version with no crew aboard, so the undocking happens on a command sent by ground controllers at SpaceX’s facility in Hawthorne, California. Splashdown is targeted off the California coast, and NASA says teams will adjust plans as needed based on conditions in the Dragon recovery area.
The picture
An earlier cargo Dragon (NASA’s caption says the 34th resupply mission) departing after undocking from Harmony’s forward port, photographed by NASA astronaut Jessica Meir. Credit NASA/Jessica Meir.
tiles.src: NASA space station blog, 18 Nov 2026 (Mark A. Garcia) · NASA media advisory M26-087, NASA to Cover 35th SpaceX Resupply Mission Space Station Departure, updated 18 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: Two days apart, same satellite: California’s Sierra Nevada goes from bare rock to white
tiles.nums: about 120 cm of new snow possible above 8,000 ft (2,400 m) in the 18 to 20 November storm, according to the US National Weather Service warning NASA cites
tiles.p1: NASA’s Earth Observatory set two images from the MODIS instrument on the Terra satellite side by side. On 12 November 2026 snow sat only on the highest ridges southeast of Lake Tahoe; by 14 November it covered most of the Sierra Nevada. Donner Pass recorded nearly 12 inches (30 cm) on 13 November and Mammoth Mountain 9 to 13 inches (23 to 33 cm). A winter storm warning above 5,000 ft (1,500 m) runs from 18 to 20 November, with totals around 4 feet (120 cm) possible above 8,000 ft.
tiles.p2: Connects to: Terra, the satellite that took both frames, stops collecting science data on 1 December after 27 years in orbit. NASA says it was designed for six.
deep: Early for the season

The Earth Observatory calls it “a widespread, early-season snowstorm” that “blanketed California’s mountains in white in mid-November 2026.” The before-and-after pair is a classic way to read a satellite image: same place, same sensor, two dates, and the only thing that changed is the snow.
The eye in orbit

MODIS is one of Terra’s five instruments, with ASTER, CERES, MISR and MOPITT. Terra launched in December 1999; MOPITT and parts of CERES and ASTER have already been switched off to save power. After 1 December the team will use the remaining fuel to lower the orbit, then power everything off in January 2027. The data stays free and public.
The picture
Terra MODIS image of 14 November 2026, from NASA EOSDIS LANCE and GIBS/Worldview, by Michala Garrison of NASA Earth Observatory; story by Lindsey Doermann.
tiles.src: NASA Earth Observatory, Sierra Snow Season Spins Up, 18 Nov 2026 (Lindsey Doermann; images Michala Garrison) · NASA Science, NASA’s Terra Mission to End, 17 Nov 2026 (Kate Ramsayer)
tiles.credit: Photo: NASA Earth Observatory / Michala Garrison, MODIS on Terra

tiles.cap: Lightning inside storm tops near Borneo, shot from orbit. Singapore glows at the left
tiles.nums: lightning flashes per second, nearly, across the whole Earth: about 2,000 thunderstorms at any moment and some 5 million flashes a day, by NASA’s estimate
tiles.p1: On 28 October at 14:20 UTC, 10:20 pm in Singapore, a crew member on the space station pointed a Nikon Z9 with a 14 mm lens at the South China Sea near Borneo. The frame, published by NASA’s Earth Observatory on Tuesday, shows several dome-like ‘overshooting tops’ rising out of thunderstorms, two of them lit from inside by lightning. On the left of the picture sit the lights of Singapore, home to 6.2 million people, separated from Indonesia’s Batam and Bintan islands by the Singapore Strait.
tiles.p2: Why here: this is what the afternoon storms in NEA’s forecast look like from orbit. The blue lights west of Singapore are probably fishing fleets using bright lamps to attract squid or small fish; scattered orange points offshore to the northwest are likely gas flares.
deep: What an overshooting top is

A thunderstorm normally spreads out into a flat anvil where it hits the stable air above. When the updraught is strong enough, a dome punches through the anvil, sometimes into the stratosphere. Those domes are the overshooting tops, and they are a sign of a violent updraught beneath.
Lightning from above

Sally Ride wrote that on Earth people see lightning from below the clouds, and in orbit you see it from above. NASA astronaut Anil Menon, on the station now, posted that lightning is his favourite sight from space, ‘like fireflies in the night’.
Try it
The next evening storm, watch the flash and wait for the thunder. From the station there is no thunder to hear, only the flashes lighting the clouds from inside.
The picture

Astronaut photograph ISS075-E-250951, taken on 28 October 2026 by an Expedition 75 crew member, provided by the ISS Crew Earth Observations Facility and the Earth Science and Remote Sensing Unit at NASA Johnson Space Center.
tiles.src: NASA Earth Observatory, Tossing Fireworks from Cloud to Cloud, 17 Nov 2026 (Adam Voiland)

tiles.cap: 200 seconds of fire at Mahendragiri: the engine for India’s next GSLV passed its test
tiles.nums: the duration of the flight acceptance hot test of the cryogenic engine that will fly on GSLV-F19
tiles.p1: On 5 November ISRO fired the cryogenic engine for its next GSLV mission for 200 seconds at the ISRO Propulsion Complex at Mahendragiri. Both the Main Engine and the Gas Generator ignited as expected, and ISRO says the steady-state performance was normal and consistent with nominal predictions. The engine now goes into the cryogenic stage of GSLV-F19, which is to carry the NVS-04 navigation satellite.
tiles.p2: Why now: ISRO calls it a flight acceptance test, a run on the very engine that will fly rather than a development unit, and published the result on 10 November.
deep: Two things had to light

A cryogenic engine has more than one combustion going on. ISRO’s note names two: the Main Engine and the Gas Generator. ISRO says both ignited as expected and that the steady-state performance was normal.
Where it happened
The test was run at the ISRO Propulsion Complex (IPRC) at Mahendragiri. ISRO’s photograph is captioned “Flight acceptance test of the cryogenic engine at IPRC, Mahendragiri, on November 05, 2026”.
What it will carry
GSLV-F19 is to launch NVS-04. ISRO’s page gives no thrust figure and no launch date for the mission.
tiles.src: ISRO, ISRO conducts flight acceptance test of Cryogenic engine for next GSLV mission, 10 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: Nothing beats light. NIST just used that to prove where a person is, not only who they are
tiles.nums: between the two verifying stations on NIST’s Boulder campus; a reply that arrives too late means you are not where you claim to be
tiles.p1: Two stations 195 metres apart on NIST’s campus in Boulder, Colorado, linked by electrical cables and ultrathin optical fibres, each send random numbers timed to reach a claimed location at the same instant. The person there measures a photon and reports the result, and the verifiers time the reply against the speed of light. Anyone sitting somewhere else is farther from at least one station, so their reply arrives late. The team repeated the exchange millions of times over a few minutes, and the light-speed limit itself became the identity check.
tiles.p2: A sum you can do: light travels 299,792,458 metres every second, exactly, so 195 m takes 195 ÷ 299,792,458 s, about 0.65 millionths of a second. That is the margin an impostor would have to beat.
deep: Where the quantum comes in

One verifier makes a pair of entangled photons, keeps one and sends the other down the fibre to the prover. The random numbers tell the prover how to measure the polarisation of that photon, and the prover reports the result. The verifiers then check how often the prover’s measurements match their own, a loophole-free Bell test that can only be passed by measuring the photon exactly as the random numbers dictate, and fraudsters cannot predict those numbers. NIST physicist Krister Shalm led the work; Gautam Kavuri is first author of the paper in Nature.
Why bother

NIST’s release puts the cost of cybercrime to US citizens at more than $16 billion in 2024, with far fewer than 1 percent of cybercriminals caught. Shalm: “Gaining access to a system can only be done by someone who can prove they are in a particular location — such as a bank — thwarting remote would-be hackers.”
Not soon
NIST says real-world use is more than a decade away; it would need quantum networks that share entangled photons between a customer and their bank.
The speed itself

Since 1983 the metre has been defined from the speed of light, so c is exactly 299,792,458 m/s by definition. NIST’s own Boulder laboratory measured it in 1972 at 299,792,456.2 ± 1.1 m/s, 100 times more accurate than the previous best measurement; the 1983 redefinition built on this and other advances.
tiles.src: NIST, Quantum Physics Can Verify a Person’s Location, NIST Researchers Show, 18 Nov 2026 · NIST, Definitions of the SI Base Units · NIST, SI Redefinition: Meter

tiles.cap: An old CD, a cardboard tube and a slit under 1 mm wide: build your own spectroscope
tiles.nums: the tilt of the CD inside the tube; the disc’s closely spaced data tracks act as a diffraction grating
tiles.p1: The Exploratorium’s CD Spectroscope: a cardboard tube at least 30 cm long and 7.5 to 10 cm across, a CD slotted in at about 30 degrees near one end, a rectangular viewing hole cut beside it, and a cap over the far end with a slit less than 1 mm wide and 5 cm long. Point the slit at a fluorescent lamp and look through the hole: the line of light splits into bands of colour. A fluorescent tube shows bright separate lines, the fingerprint of the mercury vapour inside; an incandescent bulb gives a smooth, continuous rainbow.
tiles.p2: Why it works: the CD’s tracks are so closely spaced that the disc behaves as a diffraction grating, and each colour leaves it at its own angle. Feynman writes the rule as d sin θ = mλ: the track spacing times the sine of the angle equals a whole number of wavelengths.
deep: Try these

Compare an LED, a sodium-vapour street light and a neon tube. Incandescent and fluorescent lamps can look the same white and have completely different spectra. Sunlight bounced off white clouds, a wall or paper shows the solar spectrum; with a 60 cm tube and a finer slit you may see thin dark Fraunhofer lines in it. The Exploratorium’s one warning: never look directly at the sun.
Lines that read the stars

In 1788 the Comte de Buffon said he was sure we would never know what the sun was made of. In the 1860s William Huggins pointed a spectroscope at stars and identified their composition from exactly these lines.
The grating maths

Feynman’s chapter on diffraction: a grating has several hundred lines per millimetre; the brighter beams appear where d sin θ = mλ; and the resolving power λ/Δλ equals the order m times the number of lines n. For n lines in step, the central peak is n² times a single line and the first side peak is under 5 percent of it, which is why gratings give such sharp lines.
tiles.src: Exploratorium Science Snacks, CD Spectroscope · The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. I, Ch. 30, Diffraction

tiles.cap: Rest a ruler on two fingers and slide them together. They always meet under the same spot
tiles.nums: where a flat triangle balances: one third of the way up from its base, by Feynman’s calculation; a plain ruler balances at its middle
tiles.p1: Take a ruler, a broom or any stick and rest its ends on your two index fingers. Slide the fingers slowly toward each other. One finger moves, then sticks; the other moves, then sticks; and they meet directly under the centre of gravity every time, wherever you start. Tape a blob of clay or some other small weight somewhere on the stick and repeat: the meeting point shifts to the new balance point.
tiles.p2: Why: the finger carrying more weight is harder to slide. The lighter-loaded finger slides until it passes the centre of gravity and becomes the heavier one; they swap roles until both carry equal weight, and that only happens at one point.
deep: Where things balance

A uniform object balances at its midpoint. Feynman’s chapter on the centre of mass works out two less obvious ones: a flat triangle balances one third of the way from its base to its apex, and a half-disc balances 4r/(3π) from its straight edge, about 0.42 of the radius.
Uses

The Exploratorium suggests the trick for finding where to carry a long pole, and for cutting a pole or length of pipe into two roughly equal pieces at the balance point. Tightrope walkers’ poles work on the same principle.
Centre of mass

Feynman defines it as the mass-weighted average position of all the pieces, and shows that a composite body can be treated piece by piece using each piece’s own centre of mass. The ruler and the taped weight are exactly that.
tiles.src: Exploratorium Science Snacks, Center of Gravity · The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. I, Ch. 19, Center of Mass; Moment of Inertia

tiles.cap: A phone whose camera pops out on a gimbal and turns to follow you, on a 2.6 g motor
tiles.nums: the mass of the titanium gimbal motor in Honor’s Robot Phone; Honor says the arm can turn up to 360 degrees per second
tiles.p1: The Honor Robot Phone, on TIME’s Best Inventions 2026 list, hides a motorised camera arm flush in its back. Activate it, by gesture or a spoken command, and it swings out on a gimbal built from more than 100 precision components, then tracks a face or a moving subject on its own. Honor says the system is 65 percent smaller than mainstream gimbals, the main camera is a 200-megapixel 1/1.28-inch sensor at f/1.6, and a separate H1 imaging chip, developed with the cinema-camera maker ARRI, handles video processing that the Snapdragon chip on its own could not.
tiles.p2: What reviewers found wrong: TechRadar’s Axel Metz wrote that he “could easily (or accidentally) snap off the plastic shield covering it” and called the YOYO gestures “the definition of gimmickry”; Tom’s Guide’s John Velasco found it “rather hefty at 8.75 ounces” and noted that vertical video is only a crop of the landscape frame, because the gimbal cannot turn the camera that way.
deep: Inside the arm

Honor’s launch release: a 2.6 g titanium gimbal motor, more than 100 precision components, 60 processes, more than 100 patents, structural strength up 200 percent, rotation up to 360 degrees per second and a torque density of 120 N·m/L. The release calls the gimbal both “3-axis” and “4-DoF”, so take the axis count with care.
Why a second chip

Yang Liu, Honor’s president of hardware engineering, told TechRadar: “The Qualcomm chipset offers very good performance for still image processing, but for video, it’s not good enough — for now.” The H1 chip sits beside the Snapdragon and handles white balance, tone mapping and exposure in real time, with 14-bit 4:4:4 internal processing and 10-bit ARRI LogC3 output; Honor claims 14 stops of dynamic range and 8 dB better video signal-to-noise.
The rest of the phone

A 6.31-inch LTPO OLED at 1 to 120 Hz and 6,800 nits peak, Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, a 7,060 mAh silicon-carbon battery with 120 W wired charging, a 200 MP periscope telephoto and a 50 MP ultra-wide. Price RMB 9,999 for 12 GB and 512 GB, China only; TechRadar puts that at about $1,500. TechRadar also reports it gets noticeably hot in long filming sessions.
Head to head

Tom’s Guide’s Sanuj Bhatia put it against the Insta360 Luna Ultra pocket gimbal camera: the phone zooms only about 4× by cropping where the Luna Ultra has dedicated zoom hardware, takes an extra second or two to get going, and its tracking only falls behind the Luna Ultra’s when the subject moves quickly toward the edge of the frame. He would buy the Luna Ultra.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026, Honor Robot Phone (Nitish Pahwa) · Honor, launch release, 12 Aug 2026 · TechRadar, Axel Metz, 12 and 15 Aug 2026 · Tom’s Guide, John Velasco, 12 Aug 2026; Sanuj Bhatia, 22 Aug 2026

tiles.cap: Google’s glasses: a 12 MP camera, 41 g, nine hours, no screen. A reviewer heard them leak
tiles.nums: the weight of Google’s new camera-and-speaker glasses, which Google puts at around 41 grams; nine hours of battery, seven recharges from the case
tiles.p1: Google opened pre-orders on 12 November for ‘intelligent eyewear’ engineered by Samsung and sold as Warby Parker frames from $395 and Gentle Monster frames from $449, on sale in stores and online from 10 December in the US and South Korea. Inside each pair: one 12-megapixel ultra-wide camera with HDR and stabilisation, open-ear speakers, microphones that talk to Gemini, and a battery Google rates at up to nine hours, with a case that recharges the frames up to seven times. There is no display: you hear answers, you do not see them. Weight is around 41 grams.
tiles.p2: What Tom’s Guide found: Kate Kozuch tried them at a Google demonstration this month and liked that they feel like eyewear rather than a gadget, but noticed a delay in live translation, sound leaking to people nearby at higher volumes, photos that are only ‘okay’, and a battery figure that heavy camera use will surely cut.
deep: The privacy engineering

A privacy LED lights when the camera is on, and Google says recording is designed to stop if the light is covered or disabled. There is a physical off switch. Bystanders’ faces are blurred before images reach Gemini, and Google says camera images are not saved to Gemini history or used for training or ads. Kozuch’s point: the same design that makes the wearer comfortable ‘could make it harder for someone else to recognize that recording is possible’, and how the protections work in real use is one of the things she lists as ‘unresolved’.
What it does

Live translation across more than 70 languages, turn-by-turn Maps directions spoken through the open-ear speakers, and a Gemini that can see what you see and keep answering follow-ups without a wake word. Taps and swipes on the right side of the frame control music; a physical button takes the picture. You need a Pixel 7 or newer, a recent Galaxy, or an iPhone 13 Pro or newer, and an account for ages 18 and up.
What the prototype had that this does not

At Google I/O in May, Tom’s Guide’s Jason England tried the software on a prototype with a monocular waveguide display, though reporters could not wear the glasses themselves. He reported then that the first glasses would all be display-free, and they are.
tiles.src: Google, The Keyword: Google intelligent eyewear collections now available for pre-order, 12 Nov 2026 · Tom’s Guide, Kate Kozuch, 12 Nov 2026 · Tom’s Guide, Jason England, 20 May 2026

tiles.cap: A normal Singapore November: 252.3 mm of rain over 19 wet days. The 1874 one had 521.5 mm
tiles.nums: Singapore’s wettest November on record, in 1874; the driest, in 1981, had 53.5 mm
tiles.p1: The Meteorological Service’s fortnightly outlook carries the numbers behind the month. The November normals for 1991 to 2020 are 252.3 mm of rain over 19 rain days, an average daily high of 31.2 °C, an average low of 24.6 °C and a monthly mean of 27.2 °C. The records run wider than you might guess: the wettest November, 521.5 mm, was in 1874; the driest, 53.5 mm, in 1981; the warmest by mean daily maximum was 2019 at 32.3 °C; the coolest by mean daily minimum was 1933 at 22.4 °C.
tiles.p2: Test it: the first half of this month already had a 94.2 mm day at Rivervale Drive and 35.4 °C at Paya Lebar. Watch the second half’s review when it is published and see which side of 252.3 mm the month lands on; the outlook says slightly above.
deep: The next four days

The four-day outlook issued on Wednesday evening gives Thursday to Sunday the same shape: 24 to 33 °C and afternoon thundery showers each day, with light variable winds on Thursday turning to the northeast from Friday as the monsoon sets in.
Uneven island
In the first half of November about half the island had above-average rain: Somerset was 44 percent above its average, Tanjong Katong 65 percent below. One island, two Novembers.
Why the records are so far apart

The 1874 and 1981 figures differ by almost ten times. November sits at the hand-over from the inter-monsoon period to the Northeast Monsoon: the outlook describes inter-monsoon conditions with light and variable winds in the first half of this month, and Northeast Monsoon conditions setting in during the second.
tiles.src: Meteorological Service Singapore (weather.gov.sg), Fortnightly Weather Outlook for the second half of November 2026, 16 Nov 2026 · 4-day outlook, updated 18 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: Northeast Monsoon setting in: 32–34 °C, afternoon storms. Paya Lebar hit 35.4 °C on 4 Nov
tiles.nums: of rain fell around Rivervale Drive on 6 November, the biggest daily total of the first half of the month
tiles.p1: NEA’s outlook for the rest of November, issued Monday 16 November, says Northeast Monsoon conditions are expected to set in over Singapore in the second half of the month as the prevailing winds strengthen and shift to blow from the northeast or northwest. Expect short thundery showers over parts of the island in the afternoon on most days, running into the night on a few days; on some days the showers could be widespread and heavy. Daily highs of 32 to 34 °C, slightly above 34 on a few days; around 23 °C on some rainy days.
tiles.p2: Looking back at 1–15 November: 35.4 °C at Paya Lebar on 4 November, the month’s high so far, and daily maxima above 34 °C on seven occasions.
deep: Uneven rain

About half the island had above-average rain in the first half of November. Somerset was 44 percent above its average; Tanjong Katong 65 percent below. Total rainfall for the second half is forecast to be slightly above the long-term average over most of the island.
6 November
Widespread moderate to heavy thundery showers; 94.2 mm around Rivervale Drive that day, the highest daily total of the fortnight.
Today
The four-day outlook updated on Wednesday evening gives Thursday 19 November 24 to 33 °C with afternoon thundery showers and variable winds of 5 to 15 km/h, turning northeast from Friday.
The picture
The image from NEA’s outlook page of 16 November 2026. Credit NEA / Meteorological Service Singapore.
tiles.src: NEA / Meteorological Service Singapore, Wet Weather To Continue For Rest Of November 2026 With Onset Of Northeast Monsoon, 16 Nov 2026 · weather.gov.sg 4-day outlook, updated 18 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: One male killer whale, photographed seven times across 26 years in the deep Gulf waters
tiles.nums: sightings of killer whale groups logged from 1978 to mid-2024 in the Gulf of America, as NOAA names it, over water averaging more than 2,000 m deep
tiles.p1: NOAA Fisheries has pulled together every killer whale sighting in the Gulf of America, NOAA’s term for the Gulf of Mexico, from 1978 to mid-2024: 49 group sightings, over water averaging more than 2,000 m deep, in groups averaging about seven whales, from a lone animal to 14. Matching photographs of fins and markings identified 49 individual whales, and one male turned up in the photographs seven times between 1992 and 2018.
tiles.p2: What they hunt there: NOAA’s record includes attacks on pantropical spotted dolphins in 1994 and dwarf sperm whales in 2012, a pursuit of dolphins in 2024, and tuna.
deep: Why the photographs matter

A whale photographed in 1992 and again in 2018 is proof that the same animals use the same deep water for decades, which a count of sightings alone could never show. Photo-identification is the backbone of the catalogue: 49 individuals so far.
How deep is 2,000 m

Science News Explores’ Scientists Say column on 16 November was about the abyssal zone. By its account the sunlit zone ends at 200 m, the midnight zone starts at 1,000 m, NOAA puts the start of the abyssal zone at 4,000 m and other experts put it at 2,000 m. The water under the Gulf’s killer whales averages more than 2,000 m: ten times deeper than the point where sunlight gives out.
The picture
A NOAA Fisheries photograph taken under permit 779-1633.
tiles.src: NOAA Fisheries, Uncovering the Lives of Killer Whales in the Southeast, 17 Nov 2026 · Science News Explores, Scientists Say: Abyssal Zone, 16 Nov 2026 (Katie Grace Carpenter)

tiles.cap: Every repeating flat pattern is one of just 17 types. Escher worked them out by hand
tiles.nums: symmetry groups: the number of distinct ways a pattern can repeat across a flat plane, as George Pólya’s paper classified them
tiles.p1: M.C. Escher, born in 1898 in Leeuwarden in the Netherlands, struggled with maths at school and trained as a printmaker. After finishing his arts education in 1922 he visited Granada, where the Alhambra’s tiles hooked him on repeating patterns, and his half-brother Berend, a geologist, sent him Pólya’s paper classifying all plane tilings into 17 groups. Curator Doris Schattschneider says he “had worked out a whole theory that he called his layman’s theory, so he knew which edges had to match which edges.” In her words: “It was something he discovered very intuitively.”
tiles.p2: Test it: pick any tiled floor, wallpaper or patterned shirt and find the smallest piece that repeats. Then check whether it repeats by sliding only, or also by turning or mirroring. Whatever you find, it is one of the 17.
deep: Hyperbolic circles

Escher met the geometer H.S.M. Coxeter at the 1954 International Congress of Mathematicians in Amsterdam and they corresponded until Escher’s death in 1972. Circle Limit IV, from 1960, depicts hyperbolic, negatively curved space, after Escher pored over a diagram Coxeter sent him in 1958.
The picture inside the picture

Print Gallery, from 1956, shows a man looking at a print that contains the gallery he is standing in. In 2003 the mathematicians Hendrik Lenstra and Bart de Smit reverse-engineered it and found it effectively applies a complex exponential to an image.
The impossible triangle

Roger Penrose’s “tribar” was inspired by Escher’s Relativity of 1953, though Oscar Reutersvärd had drawn one in 1934. The Dutch crystallographer Carolina MacGillavry analysed Escher’s colour symmetry in a 1965 book. The exhibition Mathematics and the Art of M.C. Escher runs at the National Museum of Mathematics in New York until 8 February 2027.
tiles.src: Quanta Magazine, How M.C. Escher’s Art Creates Bizarre Mathematical Worlds, 18 Nov 2026 (Shalma Wegsman)

tiles.cap: A drone that lands like a bird: three fingers, springs, and it grips a branch by feel
tiles.nums: test flights in the Delft laboratory, and in every one the drone grasped its perch in under 70 seconds
tiles.p1: Flying costs a drone far more energy than sitting still, so roboticist Anton Bredenbeck’s team at Delft University of Technology built one that perches. Three human-inspired fingers, set like a thumb, index and middle finger, each with three segments of different lengths, close around whatever they touch. Touch sensors, not cameras, tell the drone when to grab, which matters when clutter or its own grippers block the view. It has held branches, a traffic cone, a T-shaped piece of metal and a human arm, and can perch reliably within a few metres if there is somewhere to grab.
tiles.p2: The trick: springs in the finger joints hold the grip closed, so hanging on costs no energy at all, and a motor pulls metal cords like tendons to open the fingers again. “We just have a tendon. We pull on the tendon,” says Bredenbeck.
deep: Why perch at all
Bredenbeck’s own words: “drones are really, really inefficient flyers.” A drone that can land on a branch or a cone and shut off its motors saves its battery where a hovering one would run flat.
Singapore’s verdict

Cecilia Laschi, a roboticist at the National University of Singapore who was not involved, told Science News Explores: “It’s a good example of embodied intelligence.” The cleverness is in the shape and springs of the fingers, not in a camera and software.
Lab only, so far

In 26 tests the drone grasped its perch in under 70 seconds every time, but all of them were in the lab. The work appeared in npj Robotics on 22 August 2026. The photograph is a Delft University of Technology press image by Studio Oostrum.
tiles.src: Science News Explores, A new flying drone uses touch to perch like a bird, 18 Nov 2026 (Lily Burton) · npj Robotics, 22 Aug 2026

tiles.cap: MIT’s phrase for what a chatbot answer can create: “the illusion of learning”
tiles.nums: principles in MIT’s 2026 report on AI in education
tiles.p1: MIT’s report does not call for banning AI. One of its eight principles is augmentation, not automation: AI should be used to “augment and enhance curiosity, creativity, and learning, not automate them.” Its named risks are the ones you would expect, weaker memory and confidence, falling back on AI at the first hint of struggle, and one you might not: fewer people. MIT saw fewer students at office hours and, anecdotally, fewer in-person groups in dorms and libraries, turning to AI instead of to classmates, TAs or professors.
tiles.p2: The point: the product of school is you, not the mark.
deep: What MIT asks of its own students
Learn to write good prompts, check every output, recognise when it has made something up, and know when not to use it at all.
Why checking matters

The report warns that models hallucinate, so students need to learn when an output is likely to be made up. MIT’s guidance for research: a human is responsible for verifying the output, and AI should never be listed as a co-author.
Keep it human

The report says every subject should include a regular in-person social component, calls for more project-based work, and asks for deliberately AI-free experiences and AI-free spaces for interaction and assessment.
tiles.src: MIT Ad Hoc Committee on AI Use in Teaching, Learning, and Research Training, Aug 2026
